paragraphs.context: Dorothy lived in the midst of the great Kansas prairies,
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dorothy lives with Uncle Henry and Aunt Em in a small one-room house on the Kansas prairie. The only safe place from a cyclone is a small hole under the floor.
paragraphs.simple: Dorothy lived in the middle of the great Kansas prairies with Uncle Henry, a farmer, and Aunt Em, the farmer's wife. Their house was small, because the wood to build it had to be carried by wagon for many miles. It had four walls, a floor and a roof, and these made one room. In the room were a rusty-looking cookstove, a cupboard for the dishes, a table, three or four chairs, and the beds. Uncle Henry and Aunt Em had a big bed in one corner, and Dorothy had a little bed in another corner. There was no garret at all, and no cellar. There was only a small hole dug in the ground, called a cyclone cellar. The family could go there if one of those great whirlwinds came, strong enough to crush any building in its path. It was reached by a trap door in the middle of the floor. A ladder led down from the door into the small, dark hole.

paragraphs.context: she could see nothing but the great gray prairie on every side
paragraphs.mainIdea: Everything around the house is gray and flat. The sun has made even the house and the grass gray.
paragraphs.simple: When Dorothy stood in the doorway and looked around, she could see only the great gray prairie on every side. Not one tree or house broke the wide flat country, which reached to the edge of the sky in all directions. The sun had baked the plowed land into a gray mass with little cracks running through it. Even the grass was not green, because the sun had burned the tops of the long blades until they were the same gray color that could be seen everywhere. Once the house had been painted, but the sun made the paint come up in bubbles and the rains washed it away. Now the house was as dull and gray as everything else.

paragraphs.mainIdea: Aunt Em was once a young, pretty wife, but the sun and wind have made her gray, thin and sad. She is amazed that Dorothy can laugh.
paragraphs.simple: When Aunt Em came there to live, she was a young, pretty wife. The sun and wind had changed her too. They had taken the sparkle from her eyes and left them a sober gray. They had taken the red from her cheeks and lips, and these were gray also. She was thin and gaunt, and never smiled now. Dorothy was an orphan. When she first came to Aunt Em, Aunt Em was so startled by the child's laughter that she would scream and press her hand on her heart whenever Dorothy's merry voice reached her ears. She still looked at the little girl with wonder that she could find anything to laugh at.

paragraphs.context: The cyclone had set the house down very gently
paragraphs.mainIdea: The cyclone puts the house down softly in a beautiful country full of fruit trees, flowers, birds and a little brook. After the dry gray prairie, Dorothy likes the sound of the water.
paragraphs.simple: The cyclone had set the house down very gently, for a cyclone, in the middle of a country of wonderful beauty. There were lovely patches of greensward all about, with tall, grand trees that had rich and very sweet fruits. Banks of beautiful flowers were on every hand. Birds with rare and bright feathers sang and flew about in the trees and bushes. A little way off was a small brook, rushing and sparkling along between green banks. It made a sound that Dorothy was very glad to hear, because she was a little girl who had lived so long on the dry, gray prairies.

paragraphs.context: all were oddly dressed
paragraphs.mainIdea: Four people come up to Dorothy: three men and one woman. They are strangely dressed in blue and white, with bells on their pointed hats.
paragraphs.simple: There were three men and one woman, and all of them were dressed in a strange way. They wore round hats that rose to a small point a foot above their heads. There were little bells around the brims that rang sweetly as they moved. The hats of the men were blue. The little woman's hat was white, and she wore a white gown that hung in pleats from her shoulders. Little stars were sprinkled over it, and they shone in the sun like diamonds. The men were dressed in blue, of the same shade as their hats. They wore well-polished boots with a deep roll of blue at the tops. Dorothy thought that the men were about as old as Uncle Henry, because two of them had beards. But the little woman was without doubt much older. Her face was covered with wrinkles, her hair was nearly white, and she walked rather stiffly.

paragraphs.context: You are welcome, most noble Sorceress, to the land of the Munchkins.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The woman thanks Dorothy for killing the Wicked Witch of the East. The Witch had kept the Munchkin people as slaves.
paragraphs.simple: The little woman says, "You are welcome, most noble Sorceress, to the land of the Munchkins. We are so thankful to you for having killed the Wicked Witch of the East, and for setting our people free from bondage."

paragraphs.context: Dorothy had only one other dress, but that happened to be clean
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dorothy gets ready for the journey. She puts on her clean blue and white dress, takes a basket of bread, and sees that her shoes are old.
paragraphs.simple: Dorothy had only one other dress, but it happened to be clean and was hanging on a peg beside her bed. It was gingham, with checks of white and blue. The blue had become a little pale from many washings, but it was still a pretty frock. The girl washed herself carefully, dressed herself in the clean gingham, and tied her pink sunbonnet on her head. She took a little basket and filled it with bread from the cupboard, and laid a white cloth over the top. Then she looked down at her feet and saw how old and worn her shoes were.

paragraphs.context: There were several roads nearby, but it did not take her long
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dorothy soon finds the road paved with yellow bricks and walks fast toward the Emerald City. The day is bright and she does not feel as bad as you might think, after being taken far from her own country.
paragraphs.simple: There were several roads nearby, but it did not take her long to find the one paved with yellow bricks. In a short time she was walking quickly toward the Emerald City, with her silver shoes ringing happily on the hard, yellow road. The sun shone bright and the birds sang sweetly. Dorothy did not feel nearly so bad as you might think a little girl would feel, who had been suddenly taken away from her own country and put down in the middle of a strange land.

paragraphs.context: She was surprised, as she walked along, to see how pretty
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Munchkin country is pretty, with blue fences, fields and round blue houses. People bow to Dorothy because she helped free them from the Witch.
paragraphs.simple: As she walked along, Dorothy was surprised to see how pretty the country was around her. There were neat fences at the sides of the road, painted a dainty blue color. Beyond them were fields of grain and vegetables in large amounts. It was clear that the Munchkins were good farmers and able to grow large crops. Once in a while she would pass a house, and the people came out to look at her and bow low as she went by. Everyone knew that she had been the one who destroyed the Wicked Witch and set them free from bondage. The houses of the Munchkins were odd-looking homes, because each was round, with a big dome for a roof. All were painted blue, because in this country of the East blue was the favorite color.

paragraphs.context: Dorothy leaned her chin upon her hand and gazed thoughtfully
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dorothy looks at the Scarecrow. He is a sack head with a painted face and old blue clothes, all stuffed with straw, and he is held up on a pole in the corn.
paragraphs.simple: Dorothy rested her chin on her hand and looked at the Scarecrow, thinking. His head was a small sack stuffed with straw, with eyes, nose and mouth painted on it to be a face. An old, pointed blue hat, that had belonged to some Munchkin, was on his head. The rest of the figure was a blue suit of clothes, worn and faded, which had also been stuffed with straw. On the feet were some old boots with blue tops, such as every man wore in this country. The figure was raised above the stalks of corn by the pole that was stuck up its back.

paragraphs.context: My life has been so short that I really know nothing
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Scarecrow says he was only made the day before yesterday and knows nothing. He heard the farmer talk about his ears.
paragraphs.simple: The Scarecrow says, "My life has been so short that I really know nothing at all. I was only made the day before yesterday. What happened in the world before that time is all unknown to me. Luckily, when the farmer made my head, one of the first things he did was to paint my ears, so that I heard what was going on. There was another Munchkin with him, and the first thing I heard was the farmer saying, 'How do you like those ears?'"

paragraphs.context: This at first seemed a great misfortune, for I knew a one-legged
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Tin Woodman tells how the Witch's spell made his axe cut off his leg, arms and head. Each time the tinsmith made a new part out of tin.
paragraphs.simple: The Tin Woodman says, "At first this seemed a great bad luck, because I knew that a man with one leg could not do very well as a woodchopper. So I went to a tinsmith and had him make me a new leg out of tin. The leg worked very well once I was used to it. But what I did made the Wicked Witch of the East angry, because she had promised the old woman that I should not marry the pretty Munchkin girl. When I began chopping again, my axe slipped and cut off my right leg. Again I went to the tinsmith, and again he made me a leg out of tin. After this the enchanted axe cut off my arms, one after the other. But I did not give up, and I had them put back with tin ones. Then the Wicked Witch made the axe slip and cut off my head, and at first I thought that was the end of me. But the tinsmith happened to come along, and he made me a new head out of tin."

paragraphs.context: My body shone so brightly in the sun that I felt very proud
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Tin Woodman's joints rusted in the rain and he stood still for a year. He decided that the loss of his heart was the worst thing, so he wants to ask Oz for one.
paragraphs.simple: The Tin Woodman says, "My body shone so brightly in the sun that I felt very proud of it. It did not matter now if my axe slipped, because it could not cut me. There was only one danger, that my joints would rust. But I kept an oilcan in my cottage and took care to oil myself whenever I needed it. However, there came a day when I forgot to do this. I was caught in a rainstorm, and before I thought of the danger my joints had rusted. I was left to stand in the woods until you came to help me. It was a terrible thing to go through, but during the year I stood there I had time to think that the greatest loss I had known was the loss of my heart. While I was in love I was the happiest man on earth. But no one can love who has not a heart, and so I have decided to ask Oz to give me one. If he does, I will go back to the Munchkin maiden and marry her."

paragraphs.context: It’s a mystery,” replied the Lion.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Lion says that he was born a coward. Animals think he is brave because he roars, and they run away, but he would run from the bigger animals if they fought him.
paragraphs.simple: "It is a mystery," said the Lion. "I suppose I was born that way. All the other animals in the forest naturally expect me to be brave, because the Lion is thought everywhere to be the King of Beasts. I learned that if I roared very loudly, every living thing was frightened and got out of my way. Whenever I have met a man I have been very scared. But I just roared at him, and he has always run away as fast as he could go. If the elephants and the tigers and the bears had ever tried to fight me, I should have run myself, because I am such a coward. But just as soon as they hear me roar, they all try to get away from me, and of course I let them go."

paragraphs.context: This was to be an eventful day for the travelers.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The travelers come to a very wide, deep ditch with sharp rocks at the bottom. The sides are too steep to climb, so it seems that their journey must end.
paragraphs.simple: This was to be a day full of events for the travelers. They had hardly been walking for an hour when they saw in front of them a great ditch. It crossed the road and cut the forest in two as far as they could see on either side. It was a very wide ditch, and when they crept up to the edge and looked into it, they could see that it was also very deep. There were many big, jagged rocks at the bottom. The sides were so steep that none of them could climb down, and for a moment it seemed that their journey must end.

paragraphs.context: They now came upon more and more of the big scarlet poppies
paragraphs.mainIdea: The friends walk into a big field of red poppies. The smell of these flowers puts people to sleep, and Dorothy does not know it, so she feels she must sit down and sleep.
paragraphs.simple: Now they came on more and more of the big scarlet poppies, and fewer and fewer of the other flowers. Soon they found themselves in the middle of a great meadow of poppies. Now it is well known that when there are many of these flowers together, their smell is so strong that anyone who breathes it falls asleep. If the sleeper is not carried away from the smell of the flowers, he sleeps on and on forever. But Dorothy did not know this, and she could not get away from the bright red flowers that were everywhere about. So soon her eyes grew heavy, and she felt she must sit down to rest and to sleep.

paragraphs.context: The Tin Woodman was about to reply when he heard a low growl
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Tin Woodman sees a Wildcat chase a little field mouse. He has no heart, but he knows it is wrong to kill such a harmless animal.
paragraphs.simple: The Tin Woodman was about to answer when he heard a low growl. He turned his head, which worked very well on hinges, and saw a strange beast come bounding over the grass toward them. It was a great yellow Wildcat. The Woodman thought it must be chasing something, because its ears were lying close to its head and its mouth was wide open. It showed two rows of ugly teeth, and its red eyes glowed like balls of fire. As it came nearer, the Tin Woodman saw that a little gray field mouse was running in front of the beast. Although he had no heart, he knew it was wrong for the Wildcat to try to kill such a pretty, harmless creature.

paragraphs.context: That is hard to tell,” said the man thoughtfully.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The man says that Oz can take any form he wants, so people say different things about him. No living person can tell what Oz looks like in his own form.
paragraphs.simple: "That is hard to tell," said the man, thinking. "You see, Oz is a Great Wizard, and can take any form he wishes. So some say he looks like a bird, and some say he looks like an elephant, and some say he looks like a cat. To others he looks like a beautiful fairy, or a brownie, or any other form that he likes. But who the real Oz is, when he is in his own form, no living person can tell."

paragraphs.context: He opened the big box, and Dorothy saw that it was filled
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Guardian puts green spectacles on Dorothy and locks them with a little key. She does not mind, because the glare of the Emerald City would hurt her eyes.
paragraphs.simple: He opened the big box, and Dorothy saw that it was filled with spectacles of every size and shape. All of them had green glasses in them. The Guardian of the Gates found a pair that would just fit Dorothy and put them over her eyes. Two golden bands were fastened to them and passed around the back of her head. There they were locked together by a little key at the end of a chain that the Guardian of the Gates wore around his neck. When they were on, Dorothy could not take them off if she had wished. But of course she did not wish to be blinded by the glare of the Emerald City, so she said nothing.

paragraphs.context: Even with eyes protected by the green spectacles
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Emerald City is so bright that even with green spectacles the friends are dazzled. The houses, streets and windows are all green, and emeralds shine everywhere.
paragraphs.simple: Dorothy and her friends had eyes protected by the green spectacles, but at first they were still dazzled by the brightness of the wonderful City. The streets were lined with beautiful houses, all built of green marble and covered everywhere with shining emeralds. They walked over a pavement of the same green marble. Where the blocks were joined together were rows of emeralds, set close together and shining in the brightness of the sun. The window panes were of green glass. Even the sky above the City had a green color, and the rays of the sun were green.

paragraphs.context: So Dorothy said goodbye to all her friends except Toto
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dorothy says goodbye to her friends and goes with the green girl to a sweet little room at the front of the Palace. It has a soft bed with green silk sheets, a green fountain that sprays green perfume, green flowers, and green books with funny pictures.
paragraphs.simple: So Dorothy said goodbye to all her friends except Toto. She took the dog in her arms and followed the green girl through seven passages and up three flights of stairs, until they came to a room at the front of the Palace. It was the sweetest little room in the world. It had a soft, comfortable bed with sheets of green silk and a green velvet cover. There was a tiny fountain in the middle of the room that sent a spray of green perfume into the air, to fall back into a beautifully carved green marble basin. Beautiful green flowers stood in the windows, and there was a shelf with a row of little green books. When Dorothy had time to open these books, she found them full of strange green pictures that made her laugh, because they were so funny.

paragraphs.context: But when the Woodman entered the great Throne Room
paragraphs.mainIdea: Oz shows himself to the Tin Woodman as a terrible Beast with five eyes, five arms and five legs. The Woodman is not afraid, because he is made of tin and has no heart.
paragraphs.simple: When the Woodman went into the great Throne Room, he saw neither the Head nor the Lady, because Oz had taken the shape of a most terrible Beast. It was nearly as big as an elephant, and the green throne seemed hardly strong enough to hold its weight. The Beast had a head like that of a rhinoceros, but there were five eyes in its face. There were five long arms growing out of its body, and it also had five long, thin legs. Thick, woolly hair covered every part of it. A more frightening monster could not be imagined. It was lucky that the Tin Woodman had no heart at that moment, because it would have beat loud and fast from fear. But he was only tin, so he was not at all afraid, although he was very disappointed.

paragraphs.context: There was, in her cupboard, a Golden Cap, with a circle of diamonds
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Witch has a Golden Cap that lets her call the Winged Monkeys three times. She has used it twice, so only one use is left, and she keeps it for her last chance to destroy Dorothy.
paragraphs.simple: In her cupboard there was a Golden Cap, with a circle of diamonds and rubies running round it. This Golden Cap had a charm. Whoever owned it could call three times on the Winged Monkeys, who would obey any order they were given. But no person could command these strange creatures more than three times. The Wicked Witch had already used the charm of the Cap twice. The first time was when she made the Winkies her slaves and set herself to rule over their country. The Winged Monkeys had helped her do this. The second time was when she had fought against the Great Oz himself and driven him out of the land of the West. The Winged Monkeys had also helped her in doing this. She could use this Golden Cap only once more, and for this reason she did not like to do so until all her other powers were used up. But now her fierce wolves and her wild crows and her stinging bees were gone, and her slaves had been scared away by the Cowardly Lion. She saw that there was only one way left to destroy Dorothy and her friends.

paragraphs.context: But the wicked creature was very cunning
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Witch puts an invisible iron bar on the floor. Dorothy falls over it, and the Witch takes one of the Silver Shoes.
paragraphs.simple: But the wicked creature was very clever in a bad way, and at last she thought of a trick that would give her what she wanted. She put a bar of iron in the middle of the kitchen floor, and then by her magic made the iron so that human eyes could not see it. So when Dorothy walked across the floor, she fell over the bar, because she could not see it, and fell flat on the floor. She was not much hurt, but in her fall one of the Silver Shoes came off. Before she could reach it, the Witch took it quickly and put it on her own thin foot.

paragraphs.context: The tinsmiths looked the Woodman over carefully
paragraphs.mainIdea: The tinsmiths mend the Tin Woodman in three days and four nights. He has some patches, but he does not mind, because he is not a vain man.
paragraphs.simple: The tinsmiths looked the Woodman over carefully and then said that they thought they could mend him so that he would be as good as ever. So they began work in one of the big yellow rooms of the castle. They worked for three days and four nights, hammering and twisting and bending and soldering and polishing and pounding at the legs and body and head of the Tin Woodman. At last he was straightened out into his old form, and his joints worked as well as ever. It is true that there were several patches on him, but the tinsmiths did a good job. The Woodman was not a vain man, so he did not mind the patches at all.

paragraphs.context: There lived here then, away at the North, a beautiful princess
paragraphs.mainIdea: A Winged Monkey tells a story about a powerful, good sorceress named Gayelette. She wanted to marry a wise boy named Quelala, and she used all her magic to make him strong and good.
paragraphs.simple: The Winged Monkey says, "A beautiful princess, who was also a powerful sorceress, lived here then, away in the North. All her magic was used to help the people, and she was never known to hurt anyone who was good. Her name was Gayelette, and she lived in a handsome palace built from great blocks of ruby. Everyone loved her, but her greatest sorrow was that she could find no one to love in return, because all the men were much too stupid and ugly to marry one so beautiful and wise. At last, however, she found a boy who was handsome and manly and wise beyond his years. Gayelette decided that when he grew to be a man she would make him her husband. So she took him to her ruby palace and used all her magic powers to make him as strong and good and lovely as any woman could wish. When he grew to manhood, Quelala, as he was called, was said to be the best and wisest man in all the land. His manly beauty was so great that Gayelette loved him dearly, and went fast to make everything ready for the wedding."

paragraphs.context: My grandfather was at that time the King of the Winged Monkeys
paragraphs.mainIdea: The monkey's grandfather, the King of the Winged Monkeys, loved jokes. Just before the wedding, he and his band dropped Quelala into the river.
paragraphs.simple: The Winged Monkey says, "My grandfather was at that time the King of the Winged Monkeys who lived in the forest near Gayelette's palace. The old fellow loved a joke better than a good dinner. One day, just before the wedding, my grandfather was flying out with his band. He saw Quelala walking beside the river. Quelala was dressed in a rich costume of pink silk and purple velvet, and my grandfather thought he would see what he could do. At his word the band flew down and took hold of Quelala. They carried him in their arms until they were over the middle of the river, and then dropped him into the water."

paragraphs.context: Oh, I am a ventriloquist,” said the little man.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The little man says that he is a ventriloquist, so he could make his voice come from the Head. He shows the things he used to trick them: a dress, a mask, skins sewn together, and a ball of cotton.
paragraphs.simple: "Oh, I am a ventriloquist," said the little man. "I can throw the sound of my voice wherever I wish, so that you thought it was coming out of the Head. Here are the other things I used to trick you." He showed the Scarecrow the dress and the mask that he had worn when he seemed to be the lovely Lady. The Tin Woodman saw that his terrible Beast was only a lot of skins, sewn together, with slats to keep their sides out. As for the Ball of Fire, the false Wizard had hung that also from the ceiling. It was really a ball of cotton, but when oil was poured on it, the ball burned fiercely.

paragraphs.context: Just to amuse myself, and keep the good people busy
paragraphs.mainIdea: Oz says that he had the people build the City just for fun. He called it the Emerald City and gave them green spectacles so that everything they saw was green.
paragraphs.simple: The Wizard says, "Just to have some fun, and to keep the good people busy, I told them to build this City and my Palace. They did it all willingly and well. Then I thought that the country was so green and beautiful that I would call it the Emerald City. To make the name fit better, I put green spectacles on all the people, so that everything they saw was green."

paragraphs.context: So the Wizard unfastened his head and emptied out the straw.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Wizard takes out the straw from the Scarecrow's head and puts in bran mixed with many pins and needles. Then he fills the rest of the space with straw.
paragraphs.simple: So the Wizard took off the Scarecrow's head and emptied out the straw. Then he went into the back room and took a measure of bran, which he mixed with a great many pins and needles. He shook them together well, and filled the top of the Scarecrow's head with the mixture. He stuffed the rest of the space with straw, to keep it in place.

paragraphs.context: So Oz brought a pair of tinsmith’s shears and cut a small
paragraphs.mainIdea: Oz cuts a small, square hole in the left side of the Tin Woodman's chest. He takes a pretty heart, made all of silk and stuffed with sawdust, out of a chest of drawers.
paragraphs.simple: So Oz brought a pair of tinsmith's shears and cut a small, square hole in the left side of the Tin Woodman's breast. Then he went to a chest of drawers and took out a pretty heart. It was made all of silk and stuffed with sawdust.

paragraphs.context: Oz ordered the balloon carried out in front of the Palace
paragraphs.mainIdea: Oz has the balloon carried out in front of the Palace. The Tin Woodman makes a fire, and Oz holds the bottom of the balloon over it, so that hot air fills the silk bag and the balloon rises.
paragraphs.simple: Oz told them to carry the balloon out in front of the Palace, and the people looked at it with great interest. The Tin Woodman had chopped a big pile of wood, and now he made a fire of it. Oz held the bottom of the balloon over the fire so that the hot air that came up from it would be caught in the silk bag. Slowly the balloon swelled out and rose into the air, until at last the basket just touched the ground.

paragraphs.context: The Scarecrow was now the ruler of the Emerald City
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Scarecrow is now the ruler of the Emerald City. The people are proud of him, because no other city in the world is ruled by a stuffed man.
paragraphs.simple: The Scarecrow was now the ruler of the Emerald City, and although he was not a Wizard, the people were proud of him. "For," they said, "there is not another city in all the world that is ruled by a stuffed man." And as far as they knew, they were quite right.

paragraphs.context: The Scarecrow, who was in the lead, finally discovered a big tree
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Scarecrow walks under a big tree with wide branches. The branches bend down, hold him and throw him among the other travelers.
paragraphs.simple: The Scarecrow, who was in the lead, at last found a big tree with such wide-spreading branches that there was room for the party to pass under it. So he walked forward to the tree, but just as he came under the first branches, they bent down and turned around him. The next minute he was lifted from the ground and thrown head first among his fellow travelers.

paragraphs.context: But the strangest of all were the people who lived in this queer country.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The people in the china country are the strangest. They are milkmaids, shepherdesses, princesses, shepherds, princes and clowns in bright clothes. All of them are made of china, and the tallest is no higher than Dorothy's knee.
paragraphs.simple: But the strangest of all were the people who lived in this strange country. There were milkmaids and shepherdesses, with brightly colored bodices and golden spots all over their gowns. There were princesses with most beautiful frocks of silver and gold and purple. There were shepherds dressed in knee breeches with pink and yellow and blue stripes down them, and golden buckles on their shoes. There were princes with crowns of jewels on their heads, wearing ermine robes and satin doublets. There were funny clowns in ruffled gowns, with round red spots on their cheeks and tall, pointed caps. And strangest of all, these people were all made of china, even to their clothes, and were so small that the tallest of them was no higher than Dorothy's knee.

paragraphs.context: That would make me very unhappy,” answered the china Princess.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The china Princess says that she would be unhappy in Dorothy's world. In their own country the china people can move and talk. If they are taken away, their joints become stiff and they can only stand and look pretty.
paragraphs.simple: "That would make me very unhappy," said the china Princess. "You see, here in our country we live happily, and can talk and move around as we like. But whenever any of us are taken away, our joints at once become stiff, and we can only stand straight and look pretty. Of course that is all that is expected of us when we are on mantels and cabinets and drawing-room tables. But our lives are much nicer here in our own country."

paragraphs.context: The great spider was lying asleep when the Lion found him
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Lion finds the great spider asleep. He sees that its head is joined to its body by a very thin neck, so he jumps on its back and knocks its head off with one blow of his paw.
paragraphs.simple: The great spider was lying asleep when the Lion found him, and it looked so ugly that its foe turned up his nose in disgust. Its legs were as long as the tiger had said, and its body was covered with rough black hair. It had a great mouth, with a row of sharp teeth a foot long. But its head was joined to its fat body by a neck as thin as a wasp's waist. This gave the Lion a hint of the best way to attack the creature. He knew it was easier to fight it asleep than awake, so he gave a great spring and landed right on the monster's back. Then, with one blow of his heavy paw, with all its sharp claws, he knocked the spider's head from its body. He jumped down and watched it until the long legs stopped moving, and then he knew it was quite dead.

paragraphs.context: He was quite short and stout and had a big head
paragraphs.mainIdea: The man of the hill is short and stout, with a big, flat head and a thick, wrinkled neck, but he has no arms. The Scarecrow thinks that such a helpless man cannot stop them, and he walks boldly forward.
paragraphs.simple: The man was quite short and stout and had a big head. The head was flat at the top and held up by a thick neck full of wrinkles. But he had no arms at all. Seeing this, the Scarecrow did not fear that so helpless a creature could stop them from climbing the hill. So he said, "I am sorry not to do as you wish, but we must pass over your hill whether you like it or not." And he walked boldly forward.

paragraphs.context: As quick as lightning the man’s head shot forward
paragraphs.mainIdea: The man's head shoots forward on its long neck, hits the Scarecrow in the middle and sends him rolling down the hill. Then the head goes back to the body and the man laughs and says that it is not as easy as the Scarecrow thinks.
paragraphs.simple: As quick as lightning, the man's head shot forward, and his neck stretched out until the top of the head, where it was flat, hit the Scarecrow in the middle and sent him rolling over and over down the hill. Almost as quickly as it came, the head went back to the body, and the man laughed in a hard way as he said, "It is not as easy as you think!"

paragraphs.context: The Silver Shoes,” said the Good Witch, “have wonderful powers.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Good Witch says that the Silver Shoes can carry Dorothy to any place in the world in three steps, each as fast as the wink of an eye. She only has to knock the heels together three times and tell the shoes where to go.
paragraphs.simple: "The Silver Shoes," said the Good Witch, "have wonderful powers. One of the strangest things about them is that they can carry you to any place in the world in three steps, and each step will be made in the wink of an eye. All you have to do is to knock the heels together three times and tell the shoes to carry you wherever you wish to go."

sentences.context: Not a tree nor a house broke the broad sweep of flat country
sentences.simple: Not one tree and not one house broke the wide, flat land.
sentences.grammar: 'Not a tree nor a house' starts the sentence, so the verb 'broke' comes right after it. 'Not ... nor ...' means 'neither ... nor ...': not one thing, and not the other.

sentences.context: nor was it dark, for the bright sunshine came in at the window
sentences.simple: It was not dark either, because the bright sunshine came in at the window.
sentences.grammar: 'Nor' at the start of a clause turns the verb and subject round ('nor was it' not 'nor it was'). It adds one more thing that was not true: the house was not moving, and it was not dark.

sentences.context: they were, so far as looks go, many years older
sentences.simple: As far as how they looked, they were many years older than Dorothy.
sentences.grammar: 'So far as looks go' is a short phrase that means 'if you judge by how they look'. It is put between commas in the middle of the sentence.

sentences.context: I am not as powerful as the Wicked Witch was who ruled here
sentences.simple: She says she is not as strong as the Wicked Witch who ruled here. If she were, she would have set the people free herself.
sentences.grammar: 'Not as ... as ...' compares two things that are not equal. 'Or' here means 'if that were not true'. 'I should have set' means 'I would have set' and tells what she would have done.

sentences.context: Whether he is a man or not I cannot tell
sentences.simple: I cannot say if he is a man or not.
sentences.grammar: 'Whether ... or not' is a noun clause that is the object of 'cannot tell'. It is put first in the sentence for strong effect; the usual order is 'I cannot tell whether he is a man or not'.

sentences.context: began to wonder where she should pass the night
sentences.simple: She started to ask herself where she could spend the night.
sentences.grammar: 'Where she should pass the night' is an indirect question after 'wonder'. It uses the order 'subject + verb' (where she should pass), not a question order. 'Should' here asks what is the best thing to do.

sentences.context: such as every man wore in this country
sentences.simple: They were the kind of boots that every man in this country wore.
sentences.grammar: 'Such as' brings in an example of a kind: 'boots such as every man wore' means 'the kind of boots that every man wore'. 'Wore' is the past simple of 'wear'.

sentences.context: the farther they went the more dismal and lonesome the country became
sentences.simple: The more they went on, the sadder and lonelier the country was.
sentences.grammar: 'The + comparative ..., the + comparative ...' shows that two things change together: 'the farther ..., the more dismal ...'. When one grows, the other grows too.

sentences.context: in any other country, be it ever so beautiful
sentences.simple: Even if another country is very beautiful, people like Dorothy would still choose home.
sentences.grammar: 'Be it ever so beautiful' is an old way to say 'even if it is very beautiful'. The verb 'be' comes first, with no 'if', to make a condition. We now say 'however beautiful it is'.

sentences.context: If it required brains to figure it out, I never should have said it
sentences.simple: If you needed brains to work it out, I would never have said it.
sentences.grammar: This is a mixed conditional: 'If it required' uses the past form, and 'I never should have said' looks at what was done. 'Should have said' here means 'would have said'.

sentences.context: having in this world, no matter whether one is a crow or a man
sentences.simple: Brains are the only things worth having in this world, whether you are a crow or a man.
sentences.grammar: 'No matter whether ... or ...' means 'it makes no difference if it is this or that'. 'Worth having' is 'worth' + the -ing form: a thing that is good to have.

sentences.context: But no one can love who has not a heart
sentences.simple: Only a person who has a heart can love.
sentences.grammar: 'Who has not a heart' is an old way to say 'who does not have a heart'; there is no 'do' with 'not'. The 'who' clause tells us which person cannot love: one who has no heart.

sentences.context: if I should get caught in the rain, and rust again, I would need
sentences.simple: If I get caught in the rain and rust again, I will need the oilcan very much.
sentences.grammar: 'If I should get caught' is a polite, less sure way to say 'if I get caught'. 'Should' after 'if' shows that this may happen, but he thinks it is not likely. 'Get caught' uses 'get' with a past participle to mean 'become'.

sentences.context: I little knew how cruel my enemy could be
sentences.simple: I did not know at all how cruel my enemy could be.
sentences.grammar: 'Little' put before the verb means 'not at all' or 'hardly', in an old-fashioned way. 'I little knew' is the same as 'I did not know'. 'How cruel my enemy could be' is a noun clause.

sentences.context: but, nothing daunted, I had them replaced with tin ones
sentences.simple: But I was not afraid, and I had new arms made of tin put on in their place.
sentences.grammar: 'Nothing daunted' is a short phrase that means 'not made afraid at all'. 'I had them replaced' is 'have + object + past participle': someone else did the work for me.

sentences.context: If the elephants and the tigers and the bears had ever tried to fight
sentences.simple: If the elephants, the tigers or the bears had ever tried to fight me, I would have run away.
sentences.grammar: This is a third conditional sentence: 'If + had + past participle' ..., 'I should have run' (in the next part). It is about the past and about something that did not happen.

sentences.context: if I had no heart I should not be a coward
sentences.simple: If I had no heart, I would not be a coward.
sentences.grammar: This is a second conditional sentence: 'If + past simple, should/would + verb'. It is about something that is not true now. 'Should' with 'I' is an old-fashioned way to say 'would'.

sentences.context: so sharp was his axe that the tree was soon chopped nearly through
sentences.simple: His axe was so sharp that the tree was soon cut nearly through.
sentences.grammar: The words 'so sharp' come first, so the verb 'was' comes before the subject 'his axe'. The usual order is 'his axe was so sharp that ...'. 'So ... that ...' shows a result.

sentences.context: he gave so loud and terrible a roar that Dorothy screamed
sentences.simple: He gave such a loud and terrible roar that Dorothy screamed.
sentences.grammar: 'So + adjective + a + noun + that ...' is another way to say 'such a + adjective + noun + that ...'. The 'a' comes after the adjectives. It shows the result.

sentences.context: “I haven’t the faintest idea,” said the Tin Woodman
sentences.simple: I have no idea at all.
sentences.grammar: 'Haven't the faintest idea' uses 'have' without 'do', which is an old British way to say 'I do not have'. 'The faintest' is a superlative that means 'the least'. So it means 'no idea at all'.

sentences.context: had they not felt so sorry for the poor Scarecrow, they could have been
sentences.simple: If they had not felt so sorry for the poor Scarecrow, they could have been very happy.
sentences.grammar: 'Had they not felt' starts with 'had' instead of 'if', and so it means 'if they had not felt'. This is the third conditional: it is about the past. The result is 'could have been'.

sentences.context: would have bitten him had he not known very well
sentences.simple: Toto would have bitten him if he had not known very well that the Woodman was made of tin.
sentences.grammar: 'Had he not known' means 'if he had not known'. The 'if' is left out and 'had' is put before the subject. The result part is 'would have bitten', a third conditional.

sentences.context: many though they were, could hardly stir the heavily loaded truck
sentences.simple: Even though there were many mice, they could hardly move the truck full of heavy things.
sentences.grammar: 'Many though they were' means 'although they were many'. 'Though' comes after the adjective, and the adjective goes first. 'Could hardly' means 'could only just'.

sentences.context: lest he should run after her and frighten her
sentences.simple: Dorothy held Toto so that he would not run after the Queen and frighten her.
sentences.grammar: 'Lest' means 'so that ... not' or 'for fear that'. It is a formal, old word. The verb after it is 'should + verb': 'lest he should run'. It gives a reason for the action in the first part.

sentences.context: When they were on, Dorothy could not take them off had she wished
sentences.simple: When the spectacles were on, Dorothy could not take them off, even if she had wanted to.
sentences.grammar: 'Had she wished' means 'if she had wished'. The word 'if' is left out and 'had' goes before 'she'. It is a third conditional that is put at the end of the sentence.

sentences.context: It was fortunate the Tin Woodman had no heart at that moment
sentences.simple: It was lucky that the Tin Woodman had no heart at that moment, because it would have beat loud and fast from fear.
sentences.grammar: The sentence is 'It was fortunate (that) the Tin Woodman had no heart ...'. The word 'that' is left out. 'It' is an empty subject, and the real idea is in the clause after 'fortunate'.

sentences.context: But being only tin, the Woodman was not at all afraid
sentences.simple: But the Woodman was made only of tin, so he was not afraid at all.
sentences.grammar: 'Being only tin' is a participle phrase at the start. It gives a reason and means 'because he was only tin'. The subject of 'being' is the same as the subject of the main clause: the Woodman.

sentences.context: If he is a Beast when I go to see him, I shall roar
sentences.simple: If he is a Beast when I go to see him, I will roar as loud as I can.
sentences.grammar: This is a first conditional sentence: 'If + present simple, shall + verb'. 'Shall' with 'I' is an old-fashioned way to say 'will'. 'My loudest' means 'as loud as I can'.

sentences.context: neither the Winged Monkeys nor she, herself, dare hurt the girl in any way
sentences.simple: The Witch knew well that neither the Winged Monkeys nor she herself dared to hurt the girl.
sentences.grammar: 'Neither ... nor ...' links two subjects, and the verb is 'dare', with no -s. 'Dare' here is used like a modal verb, followed by 'hurt' with no 'to'. 'Herself' makes 'she' stronger.

sentences.context: he lay so battered and dented that he could neither move nor groan
sentences.simple: He lay so hurt and bent out of shape that he could not move and could not make a sound.
sentences.grammar: 'So ... that ...' shows a result. 'Could neither move nor groan' uses 'neither ... nor ...' with two verbs, and it means he could not do either one.

sentences.context: owner of the Golden Cap, whosoever he may be
sentences.simple: Whoever the owner of the Golden Cap is, the Monkeys are his slaves three times.
sentences.grammar: 'Whosoever' is an old, formal word for 'whoever'. 'May be' here shows that we do not know who it is. The clause says it does not matter who it is.

sentences.context: had they not thought I was more powerful than they themselves
sentences.simple: If the two Witches had not thought I was stronger than they were, they would have destroyed me.
sentences.grammar: 'Had they not thought' means 'if they had not thought'. 'More powerful than they themselves' is a comparison, and 'themselves' makes 'they' stronger. The result part is 'they would surely have destroyed me'.

sentences.context: the longer you are on earth the more experience you are sure to get
sentences.simple: The longer you live, the more experience you will get.
sentences.grammar: 'The + comparative ..., the + comparative ...' shows that two things grow together: 'the longer you are ..., the more experience ...'. 'Are sure to get' means you will certainly get.

sentences.context: I should never be found out
sentences.simple: I thought that I would never be found out.
sentences.grammar: 'I thought I should never be found out' is reported thought in the past. 'Should' is used like 'would' for 'I'. 'Be found out' is a passive verb that means 'be discovered'.

sentences.context: If it wasn’t for Dorothy I should never have had brains
sentences.simple: If Dorothy had not helped me, I would never have had brains.
sentences.grammar: 'If it wasn't for Dorothy' means 'without Dorothy'. 'I should never have had' means 'I would never have had', and it is about the past.

sentences.context: I cannot think why this wall is here, nor what it is made of
sentences.simple: I cannot think why this wall is here, and I cannot think what it is made of.
sentences.grammar: 'Why this wall is here' and 'what it is made of' are noun clauses after 'think'. 'Nor' adds a second thing that is also not known. 'Made of' tells us what stuff it is.

sentences.context: It is useless to fight people with shooting heads; no one can withstand them
sentences.simple: It is no use to fight people with shooting heads. No one can stand against them.
sentences.grammar: 'It is useless to fight' uses an empty 'it' as the subject; the real subject is 'to fight people'. 'Withstand' is a verb that means 'stand against'. The two parts are joined with a semicolon.
